A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CausalFM framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figure, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original CATE-estimation experiments on ten synthetic datasets and Jobs in Tables 1–2.

after.justification: V2 reports original standard-CATE, instrumental-variable, front-door, and ACIC2016 experiments in Section 6 and Appendix H.

M1.justification: V1's three-class treatment-effect classifier uses cross-entropy loss (Appendix B). V2 replaces it with a five-component Gaussian-mixture head trained by mixture negative log-likelihood, obtaining CATE from the mixture expectation (Appendix D.2). This substantively changes the output distribution, objective, and inference calculation.

E1.justification: Beyond v1's standard-CATE synthetic datasets and Jobs, v2 evaluates instrumental-variable settings with binary and continuous instruments, front-door adjustment with mediators and latent confounding, and ACIC2016. The IV and front-door settings were theoretical examples and future experimental work in v1.

E2.justification: V2 adds CausalPFN and DoPFN to the retained standard-CATE comparisons. Its new IV comparisons evaluate KIV, DFIV, DeepIV, DeepGMM, DMLIV, DRIV, MRIV, and DoPFN; front-door comparisons include linear, random-forest, and neural plug-in learners plus DoPFN. These methods participate in reported tables rather than merely appearing as citations.

E3.justification: The reported training cap increases from 100 to 150 epochs. Jobs is now described as an outcome-simulated benchmark, replacing v1's unemployment-task description. New IV and front-door experiments introduce instrument-generation, latent-confounding, and mediator protocols. Newly disclosed dimensions and masking details alone do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds limited robustness comparisons across datasets with varying latent-confounding strengths, including standard CATE estimators alongside IV estimators (Tables 7–8). Section 6.3 also explicitly probes front-door nuisance-model flexibility through linear, random-forest, and neural implementations. Neither version reports component ablations.

E5.justification: Both implementation appendices report five repetitions with different seeds. However, v1 Table 1 provides per-dataset standard deviations, whereas v2's corresponding detailed Table 5 reports only point values. V2 retains aggregate mean-and-standard-deviation reporting; Tables 7–8 also omit deviations despite their captions promising them.

E6.justification: Standard-CATE entries are replaced: Jobs CausalFM PEHE changes from 0.581±0.002 to 0.478±0.18. Changed model and reported outcome settings prevent interpreting this as a matched-setting gain. Newly reported results include front-door PEHE of 0.901 versus the neural plug-in's 0.889, and ACIC2016 PEHE of 0.638 versus CausalPFN's 0.239 (v2 Tables 4 and 6).

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem 4.3 and its proof concerning identifiability-violating prior mass, subject to linearity and non-cancellation assumptions. V1's general noise-parent Theorem 4.8, regularity assumptions, and proof are removed, while the linear-IV lemmas survive as Lemmas B.1–B.2. The IV running example changes its target from CAPO to CATE.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now claim trained instantiations and competitive performance across back-door, IV, and front-door settings. V1 claimed an evaluated back-door instantiation and explicitly deferred the other instantiations to future work. This substantially broadens the claimed demonstrated contribution.

C2.justification: V2 interprets its new IV and front-door comparisons as evidence of applicability under latent confounding without retraining. Appendix D.2 adds the explanation that the GMM supports multimodal effect predictions. V1's specific explanation about automatically avoiding weak instruments is dropped in favor of generic identifiability-formula selection language.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation disclosure: tokenization and query masking, transformer dimensions, GMM parameters, detailed SCM generators and hyperparameter priors, additional baseline implementation sources, and ACIC2016 access information. Reported A100 training time changes from about 10 to 24 hours. Much of this is newly documented detail rather than evidence of changed earlier settings.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations covering IV estimators, Bayesian-prior concerns, and application context, including Singh et al., Syrgkanis et al., and Linero and Antonelli. The central positioning against BBCI, CausalPFN, and Do-PFN remains substantially the same; much of the earlier related-work discussion is relocated to Appendix A.

P1.justification: Section 4 is substantially rewritten and reorganized, with the extended linear-IV motivation moved into Appendix B. Related work is divided between the main text and Appendix A, experiments are organized by causal setting, and implementation material is reorganized into detailed appendices. These are extensive narrative changes beyond added results.

P2.justification: V2 introduces an identifiability-comparison table, combines synthetic and Jobs summaries, relocates detailed synthetic results to the appendix, and adds IV, front-door, and ACIC2016 tables. Tables gain method-group separators and colored rankings. Figure 1 is resized and relocated, alongside substantial changes to typography and text-wrapped table layout.

improvement.justification: V2 improves auditability and comparative evidence through detailed generators, direct comparisons with both competing PFNs, and broader benchmarks, addressing clear gaps in v1. These gains are limited by lost per-dataset uncertainty and substantive inconsistencies: DoPFN's Table 5 entries average about 0.519, versus 0.586 in Table 2, and Appendix F makes the continuous instrument deterministic given X despite claiming conditional relevance. The net improvement is therefore clearest in documentation and comparative coverage; the expanded validation remains imperfect.
